pages.title: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
pages.content:
So far, you may have encountered and utilised the term Greedy frequently. 

However, in this module, we will delve into the concept of Dynamic Programming (DP) and explore its distinctions from Greedy algorithms.

DP isn't anything new but rather a "Smart Brute Force" approach.

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in First DP problem: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

Enumerate every subset even when N is very large.
Use an unrelated graph traversal regardless of the problem state.

pages.title: Maximum Sum of a Valid Subset
pages.content:
So, you might have used a "Greedy" strategy in the previous example. 

That is, greedily take all the positive numbers in the subset because they will always increase the total sum of the subset, and reject all the negative numbers in the subset because they will always decrease the total sum of the subset.

Let's try to solve another similar problem.

Given $N$ integers, you have to pick a valid subset with the largest sum from these integers.

A valid subset is a subset in which no two adjacent elements are picked.

**Just read the statement and think about it for now. We'll be solving this over the next few pages.**

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in First DP problem: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Possible Greedy Strategies.

pages.title: Strategy - Optimal Subset Selection
pages.content:
Since we cannot take all the elements, lets take the alternate elements.

That is take all the even-indexed numbers together in one subset and all the odd-indexed numbers together in another subset. The resultant answer would be the greater one of both.

Also, we will optimise this strategy further by always rejecting negative numbers.

Let's try to see if this strategy works or fails in some cases.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Possible Greedy Strategies: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

checkpoint.question: Why can greedy subset strategies fail? A locally attractive choice can block a better global combination.
options: Why can greedy subset strategies fail? A locally attractive choice can block a better global combination.

pages.title: Greedy Strategy
pages.content:
Since that didn't work out, let's try to take the largest element of the integers first, then the second largest, and so on.

If at any point we cannot take an element (if either of its neighbours is already taken), we will skip that element.

Let's try to see if this strategy works or fails in some cases.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Possible Greedy Strategies: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

pages.title: Another Strategy
pages.content:
To overcome the last issue, this time we would consider the largest number, then the second largest number, and only take the number if it is greater than the sum of its neighbours; otherwise, we will instead pick neighbours.

Let's try to see if this strategy works or fails in some cases.

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Possible Greedy Strategies: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

pages.title: Solution
pages.content:
Since all the strategies seem to fail here, does the decision to pick an element depend on the element's value or neighbours?

If not, then we would have to brute force all the possible valid subsets and find the maximum sum among them.

Generating all the subsets and taking the valid subsets amongst them will definitely be exponential - $2^{N}$ (Including and excluding every element).

However, we will be using dynamic programming to somehow optimise this complexity.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Brute Force solutions?: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

pages.content:
Let's try brute force for this problem.

That is, generate all the possible valid subsets from the given list of integers and select the one with the maximum sum.

Can you select answer the total number of possible valid subsets for the given input of integers?

pages.title: Solving for smaller subproblems
pages.content:
Instead of generating all the valid subsets, let's try to break down this problem.

That is, we will solve for prefixes.

So, for say, $N = 1$, we will only look for the solution to the first element.

For $N = 2$, we will only look for the solution to the first two elements. We will increase the number of elements in the prefixes as we increase $N$.

Maybe we can use these subproblems to solve for all the integers.

callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Valid Subsets and Subproblems: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

pages.title: Subset Visualization
pages.content:
Let's try to visualise the smaller groups of subset for $N = 4$

Say the input is - [1, 2, 3, 4].

The list of all the valid subsets of these four elements is -



The group of the subsets that do not contain 4 is - 



We notice that this is basically all the valid subsets for prefix of size 3.

The group of the subsets that do contain 4 is - 



Since 4 is common in all, let's take it out.



This new group is just the valid subset for $N = 2$, i.e. prefix of two elements.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Valid Subsets and Subproblems: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

pages.title: Subset Sum Optimization
pages.content:
Let’s try to solve this problem for five elements. Say the input of integers is - [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. 

The list of all the valid subsets of these five elements is - 



Since these are too many subsets, let's try to break these down into smaller group of subsets - subsets that do not contain 5 and subsets that do contain 5.

The group of subsets that do not contain 5 is - 



If we notice carefully, this group is just all the valid subsets for the prefix of four elements.

So the maximum sum from this group is just the answer for the prefix of four elements.

And the group of subsets that do contain 5 - 



Since 5 is common in all the subsets of this group, let's take it out.



Now, this group is just the valid subsets for the prefix of three elements.

The answer from this group will be 5 + answer for the prefix of three elements.

And because we have already calculated the answers for all the prefixes, maybe we don't need to generate all the possible valid subsets of five elements, we can reuse the answers to these prefixes to calculate the answer for five elements.

callout.title: Key takeaway
callout.text: Focus on the core idea in Valid Subsets and Subproblems: understand the state definition, transition, and edge cases before implementing.

pages.content:
Now, since we know the answer to $N = 5$ depends on it's prefixes, let's try to formulate it.

Say we have the answer to prefix of three element as $dp(3)$ and prefix of four elements as $dp(4)$.

Can you figure out what the maximum sum of a valid subset of five elements - $dp(5)$ exactly would be using the answers to these prefixes?
